samples.answer:
If your goal is **real conversation**, the programs that work best are the ones that make you produce language—not just recognize it.

## Best choices

### 1. **italki — best overall for actually speaking**
You take one-on-one lessons with a professional teacher or conversation tutor. You can specifically book “conversation practice,” pronunciation, travel, interview, or structured lessons. italki connects learners with teachers for personalized online lessons. ([play.google.com](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details/italki_learn_any_language?hl=en-US&id=com.italki.app&utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** becoming comfortable talking to a real person  
**Weakness:** quality varies by tutor, so try several teachers  
**How to use it:** book two 30-minute lessons weekly and ask the tutor to correct only major errors while keeping you talking.

### 2. **Lingoda — best structured live course**
Lingoda offers live private or small-group classes with native-level teachers, structured materials, and regular speaking practice. Its classes are explicitly communication-oriented and include teacher feedback. ([lingoda.com](https://www.lingoda.com/en/pricing/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** people who need a schedule, curriculum, and accountability  
**Weakness:** more expensive than a self-study app; group classes give you less individual attention  
**Tip:** choose small-group classes and volunteer to answer frequently.

### 3. **Pimsleur — best self-study program for speaking from day one**
Pimsleur is audio-first: lessons prompt you to answer aloud, with roughly 30-minute conversational lessons focused on listening and speaking. Its Voice Coach feature also provides pronunciation practice and AI feedback in many languages. ([pimsleur.com](https://www.pimsleur.com/pimsleur-faq/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** beginners, travelers, commuters, and people who dislike textbooks  
**Weakness:** it does not give you genuine back-and-forth conversation with another person  
**Verdict:** excellent preparation for speaking, but add a tutor once you know the basics.

### 4. **Babbel — best all-around app with guided speaking**
Babbel combines practical dialogues, grammar explanations, pronunciation exercises, and speech recognition. Its current Babbel Speak feature offers guided AI conversation scenarios in languages including French, German, Italian, and Mexican or European Spanish. ([babbel.com](https://www.babbel.com/the-babbel-method?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** learners who want structure but also want to practice saying useful sentences  
**Weakness:** AI role-play is not the same as unpredictable human conversation  
**Note:** Babbel Live was discontinued for private learners after June 30, 2025, so do not buy Babbel expecting regular live group classes unless you have access through an organization. ([support.babbel.com](https://support.babbel.com/hc/en-gb/articles/360059593771-How-do-I-join-a-Babbel-Live-class?utm_source=openai))

## My honest ranking

| Goal | Best choice |
|---|---|
| Speak with real people quickly | **italki** |
| Follow a complete live curriculum | **Lingoda** |
| Practice speaking alone every day | **Pimsleur** |
| Get structure, grammar, and low-pressure speaking | **Babbel** |
| Become conversational fastest | **Pimsleur or Babbel + italki** |

## The combination I’d recommend

For most adults:

1. **Babbel or Pimsleur:** 20–30 minutes most days  
2. **italki:** one or two live sessions per week  
3. **Real-world output:** speak aloud, record yourself, or narrate your day in the target language

The key distinction is that **speaking drills build recall**, while **live interaction builds conversational ability**. Research on instructed second-language learning consistently treats interaction, modified output, and corrective feedback as important parts of developing speaking ability; app-based dialogue systems can help, but their effectiveness depends heavily on how much meaningful language you actually produce. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language-teaching/article/interaction-and-instructed-second-language-acquisition/78A156EE200F744F5978F99BFB073DBE?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** If you can pay for only one thing, choose a good **italki tutor**. If you’re not ready to speak with people yet, use **Pimsleur** first, then add live conversation as soon as possible.

samples.answer:
The fastest realistic goal in six months is **functional A2 Spanish**: handling shops, transport, housing, appointments, simple work interactions, and basic social conversations. The CEFR describes A2 as managing familiar everyday communication and social contact—not fluency. ([rm.coe.int](https://rm.coe.int/commom-european-framework-of-reference-for-language-learning-teaching/16809ea0d4?utm_source=openai))

## The fastest approach

### 1. Study every day—about 60–90 minutes
Consistency beats occasional long sessions:

- **20 minutes:** structured course or textbook
- **15 minutes:** spaced-repetition vocabulary
- **15 minutes:** listening with transcript
- **15–30 minutes:** speaking aloud or with a tutor

If you can manage **10–12 hours per week**, you’ll make a substantial jump in six months. Treat Spanish like a part-time job, not a hobby.

### 2. Use one structured beginner course
Don’t combine five apps and jump randomly between topics. Choose one main spine, such as:

- A beginner Spanish course designed for **A1–A2**
- Instituto Cervantes’ **AVE Global**, which follows CEFR levels and includes interactive exercises, videos, and structured courses from A1 onward. ([ave.cervantes.es](https://ave.cervantes.es/AVEGlobal/cursos-espanol-en-linea-ave-global.html?utm_source=openai))

Use an app only for reinforcement—not as your entire plan.

### 3. Start speaking in week one
Book a tutor or conversation partner **at least twice a week**. Tell them:

> “I’m moving to Spain. Focus on practical Spanish, correction, listening, and role-plays—not academic grammar.”

Practice situations you’ll actually face:

- Introducing yourself to neighbors
- Ordering food and coffee
- Renting an apartment
- Calling a doctor
- Going to the pharmacy
- Understanding bills and forms
- Asking for directions
- Explaining a problem to a landlord
- Making appointments
- Handling misunderstandings

You need the ability to **communicate imperfectly**, not wait until your grammar is correct.

## Six-month plan

### Months 1–2: Build the survival base
Learn:

- Pronunciation and spelling
- Greetings, numbers, dates, time
- Present-tense verbs
- Questions and negation
- Food, transport, housing, shopping
- **ser, estar, tener, haber, ir, querer, poder, necesitar**
- About 500–800 high-frequency words

Begin speaking immediately, even if you can only produce short sentences.

### Months 3–4: Become independently functional
Add:

- Past tense for daily experiences
- Near future: *voy a…*
- Object pronouns gradually
- Comparisons and opinions
- Health, work, bureaucracy, emergencies
- Listening to slow, learner-oriented Spanish

Start doing one weekly task entirely in Spanish: a mock phone call, a grocery list, a voice message, or a conversation with a tutor.

### Months 5–6: Simulate your new life
Switch much of your practice to Spain-specific material:

- Spanish news or podcasts at reduced speed
- Videos from Spanish speakers—not just Latin American courses
- Apartment listings, menus, transit announcements, and government websites
- Role-play conversations at normal speed
- Weekly “Spanish-only” sessions

By the final month, practice recovering from failure:

- “Could you repeat that more slowly?”
- “I understand the general idea, but not that word.”
- “Could you write it down?”
- “Do you mean…?”
- “I’m still learning Spanish.”

## Prioritize these phrases

Memorize useful chunks rather than isolated vocabulary:

- **¿Me puede ayudar?** — Can you help me?
- **Estoy aprendiendo español.** — I’m learning Spanish.
- **¿Puede hablar más despacio?** — Can you speak more slowly?
- **No entiendo.** — I don’t understand.
- **¿Qué significa…?** — What does … mean?
- **Quería…** — I wanted / I’d like…
- **Necesito…** — I need…
- **Tengo una cita.** — I have an appointment.
- **¿Cuánto cuesta?** — How much does it cost?
- **¿Dónde está…?** — Where is…?
- **¿Me lo puede escribir?** — Can you write it down?
- **¿Hay algún problema?** — Is there a problem?

Also learn numbers, spelling names aloud, dates, times, addresses, and polite forms. Those will be more useful initially than obscure grammar.

## Use Spanish from day one

Change your phone and maps to Spanish. Label things in your home. Narrate your actions:

> *Estoy haciendo café. Ahora voy a trabajar. Necesito comprar leche.*

Listen repeatedly to the same short audio until you can understand it comfortably. Repetition is more valuable than constantly consuming new material.

## Don’t accidentally learn the wrong target

Spanish varies by country. Since you’re moving to Spain:

- Learn **vosotros** eventually, though **ustedes** will still be understood.
- Get used to Spain’s pronunciation, especially the “th”-like sound in parts of Spain.
- Learn common Spain vocabulary: **coche**, **móvil**, **ordenador**, **zumo**, **piso**, **vale**, **coger**—while recognizing the Latin American alternatives.
- Find out where you’re moving. Spanish is official throughout Spain, but Catalan, Galician, Basque, Valencian, and Aranese have official status in particular regions. ([lamoncloa.gob.es](https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/lang/en/espana/Paginas/constitution.aspx?mode=Light&utm_source=openai))

You do not need to learn a regional language before moving, but learning a few local greetings will show respect and help you integrate.

## The minimum effective weekly schedule

- **5 days:** 30–45 minutes structured study
- **Daily:** 15 minutes listening
- **2–3 times:** 30–60-minute speaking sessions
- **Daily:** 5–10 minutes reviewing vocabulary
- **Once weekly:** complete a real-world task in Spanish

The biggest mistake would be spending six months “preparing to speak.” Start speaking badly now, get corrected, and make Spanish part of your daily life.

For your situation, I’d recommend **a structured beginner-to-intermediate course rather than a casual vocabulary app**. You’ll probably recover a lot quickly once you reactivate the basics.

### Best overall: Alliance Française
Look for an **Alliance Française** near you, either in person or online. Their courses are organized by proficiency level, usually include placement testing, and give you regular speaking practice with an instructor. The U.S. network has a directory of local chapters, and many offer online, conversation, and private classes. ([afusa.org](https://www.afusa.org/?utm_source=openai))

### Best self-paced option: Pimsleur + a grammar resource
If you need flexibility:

- **Pimsleur French** — 20–30 minutes of listening and speaking practice daily; useful for getting your pronunciation and conversational reflexes back. It offers five French levels and a free trial. ([pimsleur.com](https://www.pimsleur.com/learn-french/?utm_source=openai))
- Add a grammar-focused resource such as **French in Action**, a well-established video-based course from Yale, or a French workbook. ([yalebooks.yale.edu](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/resources/french-in-action/?utm_source=openai))

### Best if you want live online instruction
**Lingoda** offers live online French classes with teachers and uses CEFR levels such as A1 through C1, which can make your progress easier to track. ([lingoda.com](https://www.lingoda.com/en/french/?utm_source=openai))

### My practical recommendation
Start with this 12-week plan:

1. Take a free placement test.
2. Spend **20 minutes daily** on Pimsleur or another structured course.
3. Take **one live class weekly** through Alliance Française or Lingoda.
4. Watch or listen to French for **10 minutes a day**—even if you understand only part of it.
5. After a month, try a short conversation rather than restarting from zero.

If you want **one answer**: choose **Alliance Française** if you like classes and accountability; choose **Pimsleur plus a weekly tutor/class** if you prefer studying independently.

**Best overall: Pimsleur Japanese.**

For a business traveler who mainly needs to **speak and understand practical Japanese quickly**, Pimsleur is the strongest single-course choice. Its lessons are about 30 minutes, audio-first, and built around listening and speaking rather than extended grammar study. The Japanese program includes 30 conversational lessons plus reading practice, and the Japanese-only subscription is currently listed at **$19.95/month** with a seven-day trial. ([pimsleur.com](https://www.pimsleur.com/learn-japanese?utm_source=openai))

### Why it fits business travel
- Easy to complete during commuting or flights  
- Emphasizes pronunciation, listening, and recall  
- Useful for introductions, restaurants, taxis, hotels, meetings, and basic small talk  
- Gets you speaking from the beginning  
- Requires less setup than a large, textbook-style course  

### Important limitation
Pimsleur will not fully prepare you for **formal business Japanese**, especially *keigo*—the honorific and humble language used with clients, senior colleagues, and partners. For that, add a weekly lesson with a tutor specializing in business Japanese. Preply lets you filter Japanese tutors by business specialization and tailor lessons to your role and professional situations. ([preply.com](https://preply.com/en/online/japanese-native-speakers?utm_source=openai))

### Best plan
1. **Pimsleur Japanese:** 30 minutes daily for 6–8 weeks.  
2. **One online tutor session weekly:** practice self-introductions, exchanging business cards, meeting etiquette, scheduling, dining, and your industry vocabulary.  
3. Learn a small set of polite phrases and practice listening to natural-speed Japanese.

### Alternatives
- **Rocket Japanese:** Better if you want a more structured course with extensive reading and lifetime access; Level 1 is listed at **$149.95**, while the full three-level package is **$449.85**. ([rocketlanguages.com](https://www.rocketlanguages.com/pricing?language=japanese&utm_source=openai))  
- **JapanesePod101:** Better as a broad supplementary library, with short lessons and dedicated travel and business paths, but it can feel less linear than Pimsleur. ([japanesepod101.com](https://www.japanesepod101.com/speak-japanese/?utm_source=openai))  

**Bottom line:** Choose **Pimsleur Japanese** for rapid conversational readiness; add a business-Japanese tutor if you’ll be negotiating, presenting, or meeting clients.

samples.answer:
The fastest route is **structured study + daily speaking + immediate immersion**—not trying five apps at once.

## Set the right target

In six months, aim for:

- **A2 Spanish:** enough for shopping, transport, appointments, housing issues, basic small talk, and simple problems.
- **Early B1 if possible:** enough to handle unfamiliar situations and maintain basic conversations.

The Instituto Cervantes describes A2 as handling short everyday texts, simple information, directions, forms, and familiar social interactions—roughly what “getting by” requires. ([cvc.cervantes.es](https://cvc.cervantes.es/ensenanza/biblioteca_ELE/plan_curricular/niveles/01_objetivos_relacion_a1-a2.htm?utm_source=openai))

## Your weekly plan

Aim for **10–12 focused hours per week**:

- **3 hours:** live conversation with a tutor, ideally from Spain
- **3 hours:** structured beginner course
- **2 hours:** listening practice
- **1–2 hours:** vocabulary review
- **1–2 hours:** speaking/writing tasks and practical Spanish

If you can only manage 5 hours weekly, prioritize **speaking lessons and listening** over grammar exercises.

## Six-month roadmap

### Months 1–2: Build the survival foundation

Learn:

- pronunciation and spelling
- greetings, introductions, numbers, dates, time
- present-tense verbs
- asking questions and saying you do/do not understand
- food, shopping, transport, housing, health, and directions
- high-frequency verbs: *ser, estar, tener, hacer, ir, querer, poder, necesitar*

By the end of month two, you should be able to say things like:

- “I’m looking for…”
- “I need an appointment.”
- “Could you repeat that more slowly?”
- “How much does this cost?”
- “I have a problem with the apartment.”
- “I don’t understand. Can you write it down?”

### Months 3–4: Start operating in Spanish

Add:

- past tense for basic stories
- future plans
- polite requests
- apartment and workplace vocabulary
- doctor/pharmacy vocabulary
- phone calls and messages
- listening to natural Spanish at reduced speed

Have at least one lesson each week where you role-play real situations: registering at city hall, seeing a doctor, talking to a landlord, ordering food, or calling a utility company.

### Months 5–6: Train for Spain

Switch much of your listening to Spanish from Spain. Learn:

- **vosotros** forms
- common Spanish expressions
- faster conversational speech
- regional vocabulary
- how to ask someone to slow down or rephrase

Do two or three weekly “Spanish-only” sessions, even if you make mistakes. Practice solving problems rather than discussing abstract topics.

## The daily routine

A good 60–90-minute session:

1. **15 minutes:** spaced-repetition vocabulary  
2. **20 minutes:** structured lesson or grammar  
3. **20 minutes:** Spanish listening with transcript  
4. **15 minutes:** speak aloud—describe your day, your plans, or a picture  
5. **10 minutes:** write a short message or diary entry  

Do not memorize isolated word lists. Learn chunks:

- *¿Me puede ayudar?*
- *Estoy buscando…*
- *Quería pedir…*
- *¿Cuánto tarda?*
- *¿Qué tengo que hacer?*
- *No lo entiendo; ¿me lo puede explicar de otra manera?*

## Use a tutor strategically

A tutor is probably the highest-return expense. Tell them:

> “I’m moving to Spain in six months. I need practical European Spanish, not academic conversation.”

Ask them to correct only your most important errors and to spend most lessons on role-play and spontaneous conversation. Record useful phrases from each lesson and review them the same day.

## Don’t neglect listening

Many beginners can read Spanish but cannot understand people speaking normally. Every day, listen to material that is **slightly easier than your maximum ability**:

- first with subtitles/transcript
- then again without
- then repeat key sentences aloud

You should gradually get used to Spanish pronunciation, including regional differences. Spanish is the official language throughout Spain, while other languages are also official in their respective autonomous communities; depending on where you move, you may encounter Catalan, Basque, Galician, or another local language as well. ([administracion.gob.es](https://administracion.gob.es/en/espanaadmon/comoseorganizaestado/sistema-politico?utm_source=openai))

## Learn “emergency Spanish” before you arrive

Put these in your phone:

- your address
- allergies and medical conditions
- emergency contacts
- landlord’s details
- phrases for police, doctors, pharmacies, and transport
- a translation app for backup

Useful phrases:

- *¿Habla inglés?*
- *¿Puede hablar más despacio?*
- *¿Puede repetirlo, por favor?*
- *No entiendo.*
- *¿Puede escribirlo?*
- *Necesito ayuda.*
- *Tengo una cita.*
- *Estoy perdido/a.*
- *¿Dónde está…?*
- *¿Qué significa esto?*

## What to avoid

- Spending most of your time on apps
- Waiting until you “know enough” to speak
- Studying rare vocabulary
- Obsessing over perfect grammar
- Using English whenever a conversation becomes difficult
- Learning Latin American Spanish exclusively if your destination is Spain

**Bottom line:** study daily, take three speaking lessons per week, use Spain-focused listening, and organize everything around real-life situations. With roughly **250–300 purposeful hours over six months**, getting to practical A2—and possibly early B1—is a realistic target, though progress depends heavily on consistency and previous language-learning experience.

samples.answer:
The fastest route is **not “study Spanish” in the abstract**. It’s to train specifically for the situations you’ll face in Spain: housing, shopping, transport, healthcare, bureaucracy, work, and making friends.

In six months, aim for **strong A2 or early B1**. A2 is enough for basic everyday exchanges; B1 means you can handle familiar situations with more independence. The official CEFR descriptions frame A2 around immediate needs and simple direct exchanges, while B1 covers the main points of clear speech on familiar matters. ([examenes.cervantes.es](https://examenes.cervantes.es/es/dele-para-escolares/examenes/a2-b1?utm_source=openai))

## Your six-month plan

### Months 1–2: Build the survival foundation

Study **60–90 minutes daily**, divided into:

- **20 minutes:** high-frequency vocabulary with spaced repetition
- **25 minutes:** structured beginner lessons
- **15 minutes:** listening with transcripts
- **10–20 minutes:** speaking aloud or with a tutor

Prioritize:

- pronunciation and spelling
- greetings and introductions
- numbers, dates, times, prices
- directions and transport
- food and restaurants
- shopping
- housing and utilities
- essential verbs: *ser, estar, tener, ir, hacer, poder, querer, necesitar*
- present tense, basic past tense, questions, negation, and polite requests

Learn useful chunks rather than isolated words:

- *¿Me puede ayudar?* — Can you help me?
- *Estoy buscando…* — I’m looking for…
- *¿Cuánto cuesta?* — How much does it cost?
- *No entiendo. ¿Puede repetir más despacio?* — I don’t understand. Can you repeat more slowly?
- *Quería pedir cita.* — I wanted to make an appointment.
- *¿Qué significa…?* — What does … mean?

### Months 3–4: Start speaking seriously

Increase to **90–120 minutes per day** and schedule **two or three conversation sessions weekly** with a Spanish tutor or exchange partner.

Every week, practice role-plays for:

- viewing an apartment
- opening a bank account
- visiting a doctor or pharmacy
- calling an internet provider
- ordering food
- explaining a problem
- asking about a contract
- dealing with a government office
- making small talk with neighbors or colleagues

Do not wait until you “know enough” to speak. Speaking is the skill that tends to lag most when people spend all their time on apps and grammar.

### Months 5–6: Simulate your new life

Use Spanish for at least part of your normal routine:

- phone and computer interfaces in Spanish
- Spanish shopping lists
- Spanish news or podcasts at learner speed
- Spanish TV with Spanish subtitles
- daily voice messages to yourself
- weekly conversations entirely in Spanish
- mock appointments and problem-solving conversations

By the end, you should be able to talk for **10–15 minutes about yourself, your plans, work, health, home, and daily activities**, even with mistakes.

## The highest-return weekly schedule

A good minimum:

- **5 days:** 60–90 minutes of self-study
- **2–3 sessions:** 30–60 minutes of live speaking
- **Daily:** 15–30 minutes of listening
- **Once weekly:** one practical role-play
- **Every two weeks:** record yourself answering the same questions and compare your fluency

If you can afford it, the fastest combination is:

1. one structured course or textbook;
2. a spaced-repetition vocabulary system;
3. regular one-to-one tutoring;
4. lots of comprehensible listening;
5. immediate real-world speaking.

The Instituto Cervantes’ course breakdown gives a rough sense of the workload: its programs list about 60 hours for A1, 90 for A2, and 120 for B1, though actual progress varies substantially by learner and by how much independent practice you do. ([viena.cervantes.es](https://viena.cervantes.es/es/cursos/niveles_y_materiales.htm?utm_source=openai))

## Focus on Spain-specific Spanish

Learn **European Spanish pronunciation and vocabulary**, but don’t obsess over regional differences at first. You’ll encounter variations such as:

- *vosotros* — informal plural “you”
- *coger* — commonly “to take” in Spain
- *móvil* — mobile phone
- *ordenador* — computer
- *zumo* — juice
- *piso* — apartment
- *vale* — okay
- *cita previa* — appointment required in advance

If you’re moving to Catalonia, the Basque Country, Galicia, or Valencia, Spanish will still be useful, but learn whether local-language knowledge matters for your specific city, workplace, and social life.

## What not to do

- Don’t spend six months only on an app.
- Don’t memorize huge vocabulary lists without sentences.
- Don’t postpone speaking until your grammar is perfect.
- Don’t try to master every verb tense before moving.
- Don’t rely on English in every interaction once you arrive.
- Don’t translate every word; learn to communicate around gaps.

## Your first-week survival script

Memorize these immediately:

> *Hola, acabo de llegar a España y todavía estoy aprendiendo español.*  
> Hello, I’ve just arrived in Spain and I’m still learning Spanish.

> *¿Podría hablar un poco más despacio, por favor?*  
> Could you speak a little more slowly, please?

> *Entiendo un poco, pero no todo.*  
> I understand a little, but not everything.

> *¿Puede escribirlo, por favor?*  
> Could you write it down, please?

> *¿Hay alguien que hable inglés?*  
> Is there someone who speaks English?

> *Voy a utilizar un traductor, un momento.*  
> I’m going to use a translator, one moment.

The key is consistency: **an hour every day for six months beats a three-hour burst once a week**. If you tell me your available weekly hours, destination in Spain, and whether you need Spanish mainly for work, school, or daily life, I can turn this into a precise 24-week schedule.

## My honest ranking

### 1. **A live tutor or small-group class — best for real conversation**
Try **italki, Preply, or Lingoda**. You get unpredictable questions, follow-up questions, interruptions, correction, and the pressure of communicating with a real person—the things apps simulate imperfectly. Lingoda offers live small-group and private classes with professional teachers. ([lingoda.com](https://www.lingoda.com/downloads/2023/02/Lingoda-Company-Presentation-Jan2023-Updated.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Best routine:** one or two 30–60 minute lessons weekly, plus self-study.

### 2. **Pimsleur — best self-study program for speaking from day one**
Pimsleur is unusually speaking-oriented: its core lessons are about 30 minutes, require you to recall answers aloud, and introduce phrases in conversational contexts. It also offers pronunciation feedback in many languages. ([pimsleur.com](https://www.pimsleur.com/the-pimsleur-method/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** beginners, commuters, travelers, and people who dislike grammar-heavy apps.  
**Weakness:** less comprehensive for reading, writing, advanced grammar, and spontaneous conversation.

### 3. **Babbel — best structured app with useful speaking practice**
Babbel combines short structured lessons, grammar, pronunciation exercises, dialogues, and its newer **Babbel Speak** AI conversation feature. Babbel Speak currently supports selected languages and provides guided, scenario-based voice practice. ([support.babbel.com](https://support.babbel.com/hc/en-us/articles/25875402999826-Babbel-Speak?utm_source=openai))

There is also some direct research on Babbel: a 12-week study found gains in Spanish vocabulary, grammar, and oral communicative ability, with study time strongly predicting improvement. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1258413&utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** people who want a real curriculum, not just conversation prompts.

### 4. **AI conversation apps — best for lots of low-pressure speaking reps**
Examples include **Speak, TalkPal, Praktika, Langua**, and similar tools. They’re useful for role-plays, repetition, and overcoming the fear of speaking. Research on dialogue-based computer-assisted learning finds meaningful speaking gains overall, though interaction and spontaneity are still less thoroughly evaluated than basic fluency and pronunciation. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772503026000575?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** daily 10–20 minute practice, especially if you’re embarrassed to speak with people yet.  
**Weakness:** AI may overlook errors, sound unnatural, or keep conversations too easy.

### 5. **Busuu — good middle ground**
Busuu includes dedicated speaking exercises and encourages learners to imitate native-speaker audio for rhythm and pronunciation. ([help.busuu.com](https://help.busuu.com/hc/en-us/articles/19367617005970-Mastering-language-skills-through-speaking-practice?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** a guided app with a bit more pronunciation and community interaction than a purely gamified app.

## What I would *not* use alone

**Duolingo is excellent for building a daily habit and basic vocabulary, but I wouldn’t make it your only speaking program.** Its exercises can help, but you still need substantial output practice—ideally live conversation or voice-based role-play.

## The combination most likely to work

For most adults:

- **15 minutes/day:** Babbel or Pimsleur  
- **10 minutes/day:** AI conversation or speaking aloud  
- **1–2 times/week:** live tutor or conversation class  
- **Every day:** listen to easy content in the target language

The key distinction is:

- **Pronouncing prompted sentences** = useful preparation  
- **Answering unexpected questions** = real speaking practice  
- **Managing an actual conversation with another person** = what makes you conversational

**Best single choice:** Pimsleur if you want self-study; a live tutor if you want the fastest route to actual conversation. **Best overall combination:** Babbel or Pimsleur plus one weekly tutor session.

The fastest realistic goal is **survival Spanish at roughly A2**—enough for shopping, transport, appointments, housing issues, introductions, and simple conversations. Instituto Cervantes describes A2 as handling everyday expressions, simple exchanges, and immediate needs. ([cvc.cervantes.es](https://cvc.cervantes.es/ensenanza/biblioteca_ELE/plan_curricular/niveles/01_objetivos_relacion_a1-a2.htm?utm_source=openai))

## Your six-month strategy

### Study 60–90 minutes a day, six days a week

Use this structure:

1. **20 minutes: structured course**
   - Follow one beginner Spanish course from start to finish.
   - Learn pronunciation and basic grammar, but don’t get stuck perfecting grammar exercises.

2. **20 minutes: high-frequency vocabulary**
   - Use spaced repetition—Anki or another flashcard system.
   - Learn phrases, not isolated words:
     - *¿Me puede ayudar?* — Can you help me?
     - *No entiendo.* — I don’t understand.
     - *¿Puede repetirlo más despacio?* — Can you repeat that more slowly?
     - *Estoy buscando…* — I’m looking for…
     - *Necesito pedir cita.* — I need to make an appointment.

3. **20 minutes: listening**
   - Beginner Spanish videos or podcasts with transcripts.
   - Listen once for the general meaning, then again while reading, then repeat aloud.

4. **20–30 minutes: speaking**
   - Start with a tutor or conversation partner immediately—ideally **two or three sessions per week**.
   - Ask them to correct only your most important errors and practice realistic situations.

5. **5–10 minutes: writing**
   - Write a short daily message: what you did, what you need, what you plan to do.
   - Get corrections rather than merely checking it with a translator.

## Month-by-month plan

### Months 1–2: Build the survival foundation

Focus on:

- Pronunciation and spelling
- Greetings and introductions
- Numbers, dates, time, prices
- Food, shopping, directions, transport
- Housing and work vocabulary
- Present tense of common verbs
- *ser*, *estar*, *tener*, *haber*, *ir*, *querer*, *poder*, *necesitar*
- Question words: *qué, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué*
- Polite requests and basic negation

By the end of month two, you should be able to give a 60-second introduction and manage a simple café, shop, or transport interaction.

### Months 3–4: Turn knowledge into conversation

- Speak with a tutor at least twice weekly.
- Practice role-plays:
  - Viewing an apartment
  - Calling a doctor
  - Reporting a problem to a landlord
  - Asking for directions
  - Ordering food
  - Opening a bank or phone account
  - Explaining allergies or medical needs
- Start learning the past tense for basic stories: “I went,” “I bought,” “I lived.”
- Watch Spanish content with Spanish subtitles—not English subtitles.

### Months 5–6: Simulate your new life

Make Spanish part of your routine:

- Set your phone and navigation app to Spanish.
- Read menus, signs, supermarket labels, and rental listings.
- Have one “Spanish-only” session every day, even if it lasts only 15 minutes.
- Practice explaining your real situation:
  - Where you live
  - What kind of work you do
  - Why you moved
  - What paperwork you need
  - What problems you’re having
- Build personal vocabulary for your city, job, hobbies, health, and housing.

## Prioritize these over advanced grammar

Do **not** spend your first six months trying to master every verb tense or the subjunctive. Prioritize:

- Comprehension
- Pronunciation
- Frequently used verbs
- Question formation
- Numbers and dates
- Polite requests
- Listening to different speaking speeds
- The ability to ask someone to repeat or rephrase

Learn to recognize **vosotros**, since it is commonly used in Spain, but don’t worry if you initially use **ustedes**—people will understand you.

## The most important habit

Memorize these communication-repair phrases:

- *Estoy aprendiendo español.* — I’m learning Spanish.
- *Hablo un poco de español.* — I speak a little Spanish.
- *¿Puede hablar más despacio?* — Can you speak more slowly?
- *¿Qué significa eso?* — What does that mean?
- *¿Cómo se dice ___ en español?* — How do you say ___ in Spanish?
- *¿Puede escribirlo, por favor?* — Can you write it down, please?
- *¿Me puede decir dónde está…?* — Can you tell me where ___ is?

These will let you keep interactions going even when your Spanish is limited.

## A realistic weekly minimum

If your schedule is busy, aim for:

- **5 hours of self-study**
- **2 hours of speaking**
- **2–3 hours of listening**
- **One practical Spanish task**, such as making a pretend appointment or navigating a Spanish website

Consistency matters more than occasional marathon sessions. At six months, you probably won’t be fluent, but with this approach you can become functional, less dependent on English, and much better prepared for daily life.

- **Want grammar to make intuitive sense:** **Michel Thomas**
- **Already know the basics and want lots of speaking repetition:** **Glossika**

A strong commute-only routine would be:

1. **Pimsleur or Language Transfer** for active speaking practice  
2. **Coffee Break** or an easier native-language podcast for additional listening  
3. A few minutes of reading or flashcards later in the day, since audio alone will not adequately develop spelling and reading

If you’re driving, set up the lesson before leaving and avoid interacting with the phone while the vehicle is moving.

The fastest route is **not “study Spanish broadly.”** It’s to build a **survival system around the situations you’ll face every week**, then practice speaking from day one.

In six months, a realistic target is **strong A2 or early B1**: handling housing, transport, shopping, appointments, basic social conversations, and explaining problems—though not fluent discussion.

## Your six-month plan

### Months 1–2: Build the core
Study **45–60 minutes daily**:

- Pronunciation and spelling
- Essential verbs: *ser, estar, tener, ir, hacer, poder, querer, necesitar*
- Present tense
- Numbers, dates, time, money
- Question words: *qué, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué*
- Survival phrases and the 1,000 most common words

Learn full phrases rather than isolated vocabulary:

- **Quisiera…** — I’d like…
- **Necesito…** — I need…
- **Estoy buscando…** — I’m looking for…
- **¿Me puede ayudar?** — Can you help me?
- **No entiendo. ¿Puede repetir más despacio?** — I don’t understand. Can you repeat more slowly?
- **¿Qué significa…?** — What does … mean?
- **Tengo una cita.** — I have an appointment.
- **¿Cuánto cuesta?** — How much does it cost?
- **¿Hay…?** — Is there/Are there…?

### Months 3–4: Start speaking aggressively
Have **three or four speaking sessions per week**, even if you feel unprepared.

Focus on role-plays:

- Introducing yourself
- Ordering food
- Renting an apartment
- Opening a bank account
- Seeing a doctor
- Calling a utility company
- Asking for directions
- Making appointments
- Explaining that something is broken or missing

Use a tutor, language exchange, or conversation partner. Corrected speaking will accelerate you much more than another hour of passive app use.

### Months 5–6: Simulate life in Spain
Switch most practice to practical scenarios:

- Listen to Spanish while walking or commuting.
- Watch Spanish videos with Spanish subtitles, not English subtitles.
- Write messages and emails in Spanish.
- Do mock conversations without translating first.
- Practice understanding different accents and people speaking quickly.
- Prepare a personal “emergency script” for housing, medical, work, and bureaucracy.

By the final month, try to complete ordinary tasks in Spanish—even if you make mistakes.

## Daily routine that works

A good one-hour routine:

1. **15 minutes:** spaced-repetition vocabulary  
2. **15 minutes:** structured grammar/course work  
3. **15 minutes:** listening, replaying short clips  
4. **15 minutes:** speaking aloud or with a tutor  

If you have more time, add reading and conversation—not more grammar drills.

## Prioritize Spanish from Spain

Since you’re moving to Spain, get used to:

- **vosotros** for “you all”
- **vale** for “okay”
- **coger** for “take/get” — normal in Spain, but vulgar in parts of Latin America
- **ordenador** instead of *computadora*
- **móvil** instead of *celular*
- **zumo** instead of *jugo*
- The Spanish pronunciation of **z** and soft **c**, often like “th” in much of Spain

You don’t need to master every regional difference. Spanish will get you started almost everywhere, although Catalan, Basque, or Galician may be important socially or administratively depending on where you live.

## What to avoid

- Spending six months only on apps
- Waiting to speak until your grammar is perfect
- Memorizing huge word lists without example sentences
- Translating every sentence word-for-word
- Assuming everyone will switch to English
- Learning vocabulary unrelated to your actual life

## Build a “first month in Spain” phrasebook

Prepare phrases for:

- **Housing:** lease, deposit, utilities, repairs
- **Work:** schedule, contract, salary, meeting
- **Healthcare:** symptoms, medication, insurance
- **Government:** appointment, documents, registration
- **Shopping:** sizes, returns, payment
- **Social life:** invitations, preferences, making plans

Also learn how to say:

> **Estoy aprendiendo español. ¿Podría hablar un poco más despacio?**  
> I’m learning Spanish. Could you speak a little more slowly?

## The most important habit

Speak badly, every day.

Your goal for the first six months should not be “sound fluent.” It should be:

> **Can I get the information I need, solve a basic problem, and keep a conversation going?**

If you consistently study daily and speak several times a week, you can become genuinely functional by the time you move.

The fastest route is **not “finish an app.”** It’s a focused combination of **daily study, frequent speaking, and immediate real-world practice**.

Your realistic six-month target is **solid A2, possibly low B1** if you study consistently. At A2, you can manage routine exchanges about familiar needs; B1 is closer to handling most ordinary travel/life situations. ([rm.coe.int](https://rm.coe.int/cefr-companion-volume-with-new-descriptors-2018/1680787989.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## Your six-month plan

### Study 60–90 minutes a day, six days a week

Use this structure:

1. **20 minutes: structured course**
   - Follow one beginner-to-intermediate course rather than jumping between apps.
   - Instituto Cervantes’ AVE Global is a structured option covering CEFR levels A1–C1, with videos, exercises, and everyday communication practice. ([ave.cervantes.es](https://ave.cervantes.es/AVEGlobal/cursos-espanol-en-linea-ave-global.html?utm_source=openai))

2. **20 minutes: listening**
   - Beginner Spanish podcasts, slow news, or comprehensible-input videos.
   - Listen repeatedly to the same short material until you understand the general meaning without translating every word.

3. **15 minutes: spaced-repetition vocabulary**
   Prioritize phrases, not isolated words:
   - “¿Me puede ayudar?”
   - “Quería…”
   - “Estoy buscando…”
   - “No entiendo; ¿puede repetirlo más despacio?”
   - “¿Cuánto cuesta?”
   - “Necesito pedir cita.”
   - “¿Me lo puede escribir?”

4. **15–30 minutes: speaking**
   - Begin tutoring or conversation practice in your first week.
   - Aim for **two or three sessions weekly**, even if they are only 30 minutes.
   - Ask the tutor to role-play situations you’ll actually face in Spain.

## What to learn first

### Months 1–2: survival foundations

Focus on:

- Pronunciation and spelling
- Greetings and introductions
- Numbers, dates, times, money
- Food, transport, directions
- Present-tense verbs
- Essential verbs: **ser, estar, tener, haber, ir, hacer, poder, querer, necesitar**
- Questions and negation
- Gender and plurals
- Basic past and future expressions

Do not spend weeks trying to master every grammar explanation. Learn enough grammar to produce useful sentences.

### Months 3–4: daily-life Spanish

Practice:

- Renting and housing
- Banking and payments
- Pharmacies and doctors
- Shopping and restaurants
- Bureaucracy and appointments
- Work-related conversations
- Explaining problems
- Making small talk

Start using Spanish outside lessons: order food, ask a question in Spanish, leave voice messages, and describe your day aloud.

### Months 5–6: immersion and repair skills

Shift your emphasis from studying to functioning:

- Have regular 30–60-minute conversations.
- Watch Spanish content with Spanish subtitles.
- Simulate full interactions: doctor appointment, landlord call, train station, job interview.
- Practice telling stories in the past.
- Learn how to ask people to slow down, repeat, rephrase, or write something down.

These “repair” phrases are extremely valuable:

- **No he entendido.**
- **¿Puede repetirlo, por favor?**
- **Más despacio, por favor.**
- **¿Qué significa ___?**
- **¿Me lo puede escribir?**
- **Entonces, ¿quiere decir que…?**

## Learn Spain-specific Spanish

Use pronunciation and vocabulary from Spain from the beginning. You don’t need to prioritize every regional variation, but you should become familiar with:

- **vosotros/vosotras** — common in informal plural speech in Spain
- **coger** — ordinary in Spain, though it has a different connotation in some Latin American countries
- **móvil** rather than celular
- **ordenador** rather than computadora
- **zumo** rather than jugo
- **coche** rather than carro/auto

You can postpone mastering **vosotros** if it overwhelms you, but learn to recognize it early.

## A practical weekly schedule

- **Monday–Friday:** 60–90 minutes of study/listening
- **Two or three days:** 30-minute tutor or conversation session
- **One day:** Spanish-only practical task
- **Every day:** say or write five original sentences
- **Every week:** record yourself speaking for two minutes and compare it with the previous week

A structured Cervantes course can be useful if you want a defined curriculum; AVE Global’s individual courses are listed as approximately 30 hours each, with shorter lesson options also available. ([ave.cervantes.es](https://ave.cervantes.es/en/content/what-ave-global?utm_source=openai))

## What not to do

- Don’t wait until you “know enough” to speak.
- Don’t use five different apps simultaneously.
- Don’t memorize huge vocabulary lists without example sentences.
- Don’t translate every sentence word-for-word.
- Don’t focus on perfect grammar before practicing conversations.
- Don’t rely on English-speaking expats for your first months in Spain.

## Your minimum emergency toolkit

Before moving, be able to:

- Introduce yourself and explain where you live
- Order food and ask about ingredients
- Buy transport tickets
- Ask for and understand basic directions
- Make appointments
- Explain a medical problem
- Discuss rent, utilities, and repairs
- Handle numbers, dates, times, and prices
- Say that you don’t understand and get the person to repeat or write it down

**Best single formula:** hire a tutor twice a week, follow one structured course, listen every day, and force yourself to speak from week one. Consistency for six months will matter much more than finding the “perfect” app.

samples.answer:
The fastest route is **not “study Spanish” broadly**. It’s to train specifically for the situations you’ll face in Spain: housing, transport, shopping, doctors, bureaucracy, work, neighbors, and small talk.

In six months, aim for **strong A2 or early B1**. A2 covers routine exchanges and immediate needs; B1 is closer to handling most ordinary travel and daily-life situations, with hesitation. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european-framework-reference-languages/table-3-cefr-3.3-common-reference-levels-qualitative-aspects-of-spoken-language-use?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))

## Your weekly target

Aim for:

- **60–90 minutes a day, 6 days a week**
- **2–3 live speaking sessions per week**, ideally with a tutor from Spain
- Spanish audio every day, even when you only understand part of it
- One “real-life mission” each week: role-play renting an apartment, making a doctor’s appointment, returning an item, etc.

That gives you roughly **230–350 focused hours** before you move—enough to become functional if you practice consistently.

## Daily routine

A good 75-minute session:

1. **15 minutes — spaced vocabulary**
   - Learn useful phrases, not isolated words.
   - Example: *¿Me puede ayudar?* rather than only *ayudar*.

2. **20 minutes — structured course or grammar**
   Focus on:
   - present, past, and near-future tenses
   - questions and negation
   - pronouns
   - gender and adjective agreement
   - common prepositions
   - commands and polite requests

3. **20 minutes — listening**
   Use slow learner audio first, then ordinary Spanish from Spain. Listen repeatedly to the same short material until you can recognize the words.

4. **20 minutes — speaking**
   Speak aloud, record yourself, describe your day, or practice with a tutor. Do not wait until you “know enough.”

## Six-month plan

### Month 1: Survival foundations

Learn to:

- introduce yourself
- spell your name and give your address
- order food and coffee
- ask prices and directions
- understand numbers, dates, times, and money
- say what you need and don’t understand
- use basic present-tense verbs

Memorize these immediately:

- *No entiendo.* — I don’t understand.
- *¿Puede repetirlo, por favor?* — Can you repeat that?
- *¿Puede hablar más despacio?* — Can you speak more slowly?
- *¿Cómo se dice ___ en español?* — How do you say ___ in Spanish?
- *Estoy aprendiendo español.* — I’m learning Spanish.
- *Necesito ayuda con ___.* — I need help with ___.
- *Quisiera ___.* — I would like ___.
- *¿Cuánto cuesta?* — How much does it cost?
- *¿Dónde está ___?* — Where is ___?

### Months 2–3: Build a usable core

Prioritize:

- the 1,000–1,500 most useful words
- common irregular verbs: *ser, estar, tener, ir, hacer, poder, querer, venir*
- past events: *ayer fui…*, *he comprado…*
- future plans: *voy a buscar…*
- apartment and employment vocabulary
- health, food, transportation, banking, and shopping

Have regular conversations, even if they are painfully simple. Your goal is to become comfortable saying imperfect things.

### Months 4–5: Spain-specific practice

Shift from textbook exercises to real tasks:

- listen to Spanish from Spain
- practice *vosotros*, but don’t obsess over it initially
- role-play calls to landlords, clinics, utilities, and government offices
- read menus, signs, rental listings, forms, and messages
- spend one day a week with no English media
- arrange language exchanges or tutor sessions where the other person speaks normally but can slow down when needed

Learn “repair phrases” so conversations don’t collapse:

- *¿Se refiere a…?* — Do you mean…?
- *Entonces, ¿tengo que…?* — So, do I have to…?
- *Déjeme pensarlo un momento.* — Let me think for a moment.
- *¿Me lo puede escribir?* — Can you write it down?
- *¿Puede mandármelo por mensaje?* — Can you send it to me by message?

### Month 6: Simulate your new life

Each week, rehearse scenarios such as:

- viewing an apartment
- reporting a plumbing problem
- going to a pharmacy
- making a doctor’s appointment
- opening a bank account
- asking for help at a train station
- explaining your work and background
- having dinner with Spanish-speaking people

At this point, stop trying to translate every sentence. Practice getting your meaning across using simpler words.

## What to avoid

- Spending months on grammar before speaking
- Memorizing huge themed word lists
- Using only an app
- Studying Latin American Spanish exclusively if you’ll live in Spain
- Switching to English whenever a conversation becomes difficult
- Expecting to understand fast native speech immediately

You do **not** need perfect grammar before moving. You need to be able to ask for repetition, clarify information, use simpler wording, and keep going.

## Best strategy in one sentence

**Take one structured course, speak with a tutor three times a week, listen daily, and organize everything around the real situations you’ll encounter in Spain.**

If you can maintain that routine for six months, you should be able to manage ordinary daily transactions and begin building fluency after you arrive.

### 2. **Pimsleur — best self-study speaking course**
Pimsleur is unusually effective for beginners because the lessons repeatedly prompt you to **listen, recall, and answer aloud**. Its core lessons are conversation-based and audio-first, with role-play and pronunciation feedback. ([pimsleur.com](https://www.pimsleur.com/the-pimsleur-method/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** commuting, travel, and people who dislike textbooks.

**Best for:** learners who want a more organized course than a game-like app.  
**Weakness:** pronunciation feedback is not the same as talking with a human.

### 4. **Duolingo Max — best for low-pressure AI conversation**
Regular Duolingo is useful for building a habit and basic vocabulary, but the speaking value improves substantially with **Video Call** and speaking-focused exercises. Video Call provides guided or more open-ended AI conversation practice, and Duolingo reports research showing improvement in speaking performance among regular users. ([blog.duolingo.com](https://blog.duolingo.com/beginner-video-call-with-falstaff/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** anxious beginners who freeze when talking to people.  
**Weakness:** AI conversation can prepare you for speaking, but it cannot fully replace unpredictable human interaction.

### 5. **Lingoda — best for live group classes**
Lingoda offers scheduled live classes with teachers, so you have to speak in a real-time class setting. It’s a good middle ground between an app and private tutoring, though your speaking time will depend on class size and teacher. - **Live tutor:** 1–2 times weekly

If you can choose only one:

- **Self-study only:** choose Pimsleur.
- **You want structure plus pronunciation practice:** choose Babbel.
- **You’re nervous about speaking:** start with Duolingo Max or Babbel Speak, then move to a human tutor.

The key test is simple: **after a lesson, did you spend substantial time constructing your own sentences aloud?** If not, the program may be teaching you about the language without training you to speak it.

The fastest realistic target is **strong A2 Spanish** by the time you move: enough for shopping, housing, transport, appointments, basic bureaucracy, and short conversations. A2 specifically covers simple routine exchanges and immediate needs. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european-framework-reference-languages/table-1-%20cefr-3.3-common-reference-levels-global-scale?utm_source=openai))

## Your six-month plan

### Every day: 60–90 minutes
Prioritize **speaking and comprehension**, not completing an app course.

1. **20 minutes — structured course**
   - Work through one beginner Spanish course systematically.
   - Learn pronunciation, present tense, essential past tense, question forms, and common sentence patterns.

2. **15 minutes — spaced-repetition vocabulary**
   - Use flashcards with **complete phrases**, not isolated words.
   - Example:  
     - *¿Cuánto cuesta?* — How much does it cost?  
     - *Estoy buscando un piso.* — I’m looking for an apartment.  
     - *No entiendo, ¿puede repetirlo más despacio?* — I don’t understand; can you repeat more slowly?

3. **20 minutes — listening**
   - Use beginner-level Spanish with transcripts.
   - Listen once for the gist, again while reading, then repeat aloud.

4. **15–30 minutes — speaking**
   - Speak with a tutor, conversation partner, or voice-based AI.
   - Do not wait until you “know enough.” Speaking early is essential.

### Three times per week
Have a **30–45-minute conversation lesson** with a tutor. Tell them you are moving to Spain and want role-plays for:

- Renting an apartment
- Going to the pharmacy or doctor
- Ordering food
- Making appointments
- Talking to a landlord
- Handling deliveries and utilities
- Asking for directions
- Explaining a problem
- Basic workplace conversations

## Month-by-month progression

### Months 1–2: Survival foundations
Learn:

- Pronunciation and spelling
- Greetings and introductions
- Numbers, dates, time, prices
- Food, transport, directions
- *ser*, *estar*, *tener*, *hay*, *querer*, *poder*, *necesitar*
- Present-tense verbs
- Question words: *qué, cuándo, dónde, cómo, cuánto, por qué*

Goal: handle memorized but flexible everyday interactions.

### Months 3–4: Functional independence
Add:

- Past tense for basic stories
- Future expressions: *voy a…*
- Housing, work, health, banking, shopping
- Explaining symptoms and problems
- Asking people to repeat or slow down
- Listening to ordinary—but still clear—Spanish

Start doing one weekly activity entirely in Spanish: a lesson, meetup, cooking class, or online conversation.

### Months 5–6: Spain simulation
Shift from “studying Spanish” to **rehearsing your new life**.

Each week, simulate:

- Calling a doctor
- Viewing an apartment
- Asking about a contract
- Returning an item
- Reporting a lost card
- Getting a transport pass
- Introducing yourself to neighbors
- Making small talk

Record yourself answering common questions. Practice until you can respond without translating word-for-word.

## Learn Spanish from Spain—but don’t obsess over regional differences

Use Spain-oriented listening material and become familiar with:

- **vosotros** — informal plural “you”
- **vale** — okay
- **coger** — to take/catch; normal in Spain
- **ordenador** — computer
- **móvil** — cellphone
- **piso** — apartment
- **zumo** — juice
- The “th” sound in much of Spain for **z** and **c** before *e/i*

You do not need perfect regional pronunciation. Being understandable and able to ask for clarification matters more.

## The highest-return habits

- Learn the **1,000–1,500 most useful words**, but always in phrases.
- Memorize “repair” phrases:
  - *¿Puede hablar más despacio?*
  - *¿Cómo se dice…?*
  - *¿Qué significa…?*
  - *¿Puede escribirlo, por favor?*
  - *Entiendo un poco, pero todavía estoy aprendiendo.*
- Use subtitles in Spanish, not English.
- Keep your phone and navigation apps in Spanish.
- Narrate your day aloud: *Ahora voy al supermercado. Necesito comprar…*
- Have at least one real conversation every day, even if it is only five minutes.
- Do not spend most of your time memorizing grammar explanations.

## A practical weekly minimum

Aim for:

- **5–7 hours** structured study
- **2–3 hours** listening
- **2–3 hours** speaking
- Daily flashcards and short exposure

That is roughly **10–12 focused hours per week**. With that consistency, reaching a useful A2 level is a reasonable goal; the Instituto Cervantes describes A2 as handling basic everyday conversations and immediate needs. ([estocolmo.cervantes.es](https://estocolmo.cervantes.es/es/cursos_espanol/estudiantes_espanol/cursos_generales_espanol/generales_inicial_a2_espanol.htm?utm_source=openai))

**If you do only three things:** take a structured course, get a tutor three times a week, and practice real-life scenarios aloud every day.
